newsitem.title: JAPAN: Business sentiment improving in western Japan--BOJ.
newsitem.headline: Business sentiment improving in western Japan--BOJ.

text.p: Overall business sentiment is improving in western Japan, but gaps in sentiment among industries are widening, a senior Bank of Japan (BOJ) official told reporters on Monday.

"Economic sentiment as a whole is improving...but the gap (among industries) is widening," said Eichiro Kinoshita, executive director and general manager of the BOJ's Osaka branch office in western Japan.

Large manufacturers are growing confident about mid- to long-term business prospects. The weaker yen has made Japanese products more price competitive globally and business restructuring efforts also support the confidence, he said.
Key areas in western Japan include Kobe in Hyogo prefecture and Kyoto, Nara, and Osaka prefectures.
Home electronic goods makers are especially enjoying good sales by offering new products and cheaper prices, he said.
But business sentiment among apparel makers and the construction, real estate, wholesale and service-related industries is rather gloomy, Kinoshita said.
Some of them are even saying business is expected to worsen as they cannot shift rises in raw material prices from the weaker yen to retail prices, he said.

Increased demand before the consumption tax rise to five percent from three percent from April 1 could be seen as well as a subsequent retreat in demand. But it is too early to judge the overall trend of private consumption, he said.

However, Osaka's firmer economy is unlikely to weaken suddenly during the April to June period, as any fall in output stemming from weaker demand is likely to be smaller than expected, helped by spillover demand from the January to March period, Kinoshita said.

Large manufacturers, especially electronics makers, are eager to boost corporate capital spending, compared to non-manufacturers, such as those in telecommunications and retail, which face a drop in capital investment, he said.
The yen's weakness is gradually boosting exports from the area, but companies are not yet indulging in an export drive, he said.
Rather, the weaker yen is giving the manufacturing companies breathing space in case demand at home becomes sluggish.
But other firms fear a further fall in the yen would worsen business as they would be unable to shift higher import prices to their retail prices, he said.
Although difficulties facing financial firms may be dampening sentiment, it has not gone so far as to severely damage the real economy, he said.
Failures at some financial firms have not triggered a chain of bankruptcies and the negative impact has been limited thanks to other banks shouldering the failed firms' debts, he said.
Yoshiharu Obata, branch manager for Nagoya in central Japan, said a favourable economic cycle where production leads to increased income and to more spending, is at work in the region.
Obata said the region was not dependent on car exports for its economic recovery, but rather on domestic car demand and good capital investment.
Nagoya is a major car production centre.

Obata, as well as branch managers from Sapporo in northern Japan and Fukuoka in southern Japan, agreed that that consumption tax hike was unlikely to have a lingering negative effect on private consumption.
